nodes.title: Command-line tooling: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Most exam workflows involve `aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, or `kubectl`. Knowing the structure of each (resource → command → flags) saves you in the lab portion and in real life. They're all roughly the same shape with different naming conventions.

flashcards.front: How do you authenticate the AWS CLI?
flashcards.back: `aws configure` writes credentials to `~/.aws/credentials` (access key + secret) and `~/.aws/config` (region, output format). Use named profiles for multi-account: `aws s3 ls --profile prod`. Prefer `aws configure sso` or temporary STS credentials over long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does `kubectl get` do, and what flags are essential?
flashcards.back: Lists resources of a kind: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get nodes`. Key flags: `-n <namespace>` (default is `default`), `-o wide` (more columns), `-o yaml` (full manifest), `--watch` (live updates), `-l label=value` (filter by label).

flashcards.front: Output formatting — JSON, table, text?
flashcards.back: AWS / Azure / gcloud all support `--output json|text|table|yaml`. JSON is for piping into `jq` for scripts. Table is for humans browsing in the terminal. Always set a default in your config so you don't squint at JSON when browsing.

flashcards.front: How do you find a command's options without leaving the terminal?
flashcards.back: `aws <service> <command> help` (or `--help`), `kubectl <verb> --help`, `az <group> <command> --help`. These open built-in docs with every flag listed. Searching the official web docs is for concepts; for syntax, the local help is always current.

nodes.title: Dockerfiles and image building: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building a container image — a sequence of instructions that produce immutable, layered, portable artifacts. The exam wants you to know which instructions create layers, how the cache works, and how to keep images small and secure.

flashcards.front: Which Dockerfile instructions create a new layer?
flashcards.back: RUN, COPY, ADD each create a new read-only layer in the image. CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV, WORKDIR, EXPOSE update image metadata but don't create layers. Layer count affects image size and build cache hit rate.

flashcards.front: Multi-stage builds — what's the point?
flashcards.back: First stage installs build tools (compilers, package managers) and produces an artifact. Second stage copies ONLY the artifact into a minimal runtime image. Final image is tiny (no build deps) and surface-area for vulnerabilities is small. Standard pattern for Go, Java, Node production builds.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
flashcards.back: ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs. CMD provides default arguments (overridable at `docker run` time). The two combine: ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"] + CMD ["-g", "daemon off;"]. Override at runtime: `docker run myimg -h` runs `nginx -h`. Use ENTRYPOINT to lock in 'what this container IS'.

flashcards.front: Why pin base image versions instead of `:latest`?
flashcards.back: `latest` is a moving target — your build is non-reproducible. Today's `python:latest` might be 3.12; next month it's 3.13 and your code breaks subtly. Pin to a specific tag (`python:3.12-slim`) or, for compliance, a digest (`python@sha256:...`). Update intentionally, not by accident.

nodes.title: Docker Swarm (DCA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in container orchestrator — simpler than Kubernetes, natively integrated with the Docker CLI. The DCA exam tests manager/worker topology, service definitions, overlay networks for cross-node communication, and Raft consensus for leader election.

flashcards.front: Manager node vs worker node — what does each do?
flashcards.back: Manager nodes maintain cluster state using Raft consensus, schedule tasks onto workers, and serve the Swarm API (docker service commands). Worker nodes receive task assignments from managers and run the containers. Managers can also run workloads unless `--availability=drain` excludes them. A Swarm should have an odd number of managers (1, 3, 5) — Raft needs (N/2)+1 quorum to elect a leader.

flashcards.front: What is a Swarm service vs a task?
flashcards.back: A service is the desired-state declaration: image, replicas, ports, resources (e.g., `docker service create --replicas 3 nginx`). A task is one running instance of the service assigned to a specific node — it maps to a single container. If a task fails, Swarm schedules a replacement. Services are the unit you manage; tasks are what Swarm creates automatically.

flashcards.front: Overlay network — what problem does it solve in Swarm?
flashcards.back: Containers on different nodes have different docker0 bridge IPs — they can't talk to each other natively. An overlay network creates a virtual L2 network spanning all nodes using VXLAN encapsulation. Containers attached to the same overlay network can reach each other by service name via Swarm's built-in DNS; traffic is encrypted with AES-256 when you add `--opt encrypted`.

flashcards.front: Raft consensus — how many managers can you lose before the cluster is unavailable?
flashcards.back: Raft requires a majority (quorum) of managers to be reachable. With 3 managers, quorum = 2; you can lose 1. With 5 managers, quorum = 3; you can lose 2. If quorum is lost, Swarm stops accepting cluster state changes (new service deploys fail) but existing containers keep running. Recover by restarting lost managers or force-promoting a worker.

questions.q: A Docker host is about to become the FIRST manager of a new Swarm cluster. The admin runs a single command on that host: it generates the join tokens for future manager + worker nodes, initialises the Raft cluster, and the current node becomes the leader. Which command?
choices: `docker swarm create --advertise-addr IP`
`docker cluster create --mode manager`
`docker swarm start --manager`
`docker swarm init [--advertise-addr <ip>]`
questions.explanation: `docker swarm init` initializes a new Swarm and promotes the current node to manager. On machines with multiple network interfaces, add `--advertise-addr IP` to specify the manager's address for other nodes to join. After init, Docker outputs a `docker swarm join --token` command for adding worker nodes.

questions.q: In Docker Swarm: a SERVICE is a DECLARATIVE deployment description — image, replica count, resources, networks, secrets, restart policy. The Swarm scheduler converts that into TASKS — each task is ONE container instance on a node. Tasks are the imperative scheduling unit; services are the desired state. Which describes the difference?
choices: A service defines the desired state (image,
Tasks hold persistent state while services are stateless scheduling units
A service runs exactly one container while a task groups multiple replicas
Service and task are synonyms in Swarm
questions.explanation: A Swarm service declares desired state: which image to run, how many replicas, resource limits, placement constraints, update policies, etc. The Swarm manager decomposes the service into tasks — each task maps to exactly one container on one node. If a task fails, the manager creates a replacement task to maintain desired replica count. replicas, ports, constraints); a task is the atomic unit of scheduling — one container instance running the service on a specific node

questions.q: A running Swarm service `webapp` currently has 3 replicas. The team wants to scale it to 5. The Swarm scheduler will start 2 more tasks on appropriate nodes. Which command syntax?
choices: `docker swarm scale webapp 5`
`docker service resize webapp --replicas=5`
`docker service update webapp --count=5`
`docker service scale webapp=5` — the canonical scale syntax for a single service
questions.explanation: `docker service scale webapp=5` sets the replica count for the 'webapp' service to 5. You can scale multiple services at once: `docker service scale webapp=5 api=3`. Alternatively: `docker service update --replicas=5 webapp`. The Swarm manager will schedule new tasks on available nodes or terminate tasks if scaling down.

questions.q: A Swarm service update is in progress and some tasks have failed (image broken). Without intervention Swarm would keep replacing healthy old tasks with broken new tasks. Which `docker service update` flag PAUSES the update on failure so the operator can investigate?
choices: `--failure-action=stop`
`--update-failure-action=pause`
`--rollback-on-failure=true`
`--update-policy=halt`
questions.explanation: `--update-failure-action=pause` stops the rolling update when a task fails, allowing operators to investigate. Other values: `continue` (default: keep updating even if tasks fail), `rollback` (automatically revert to the previous service spec). Combine with `--update-monitor` (time to observe a task before considering it healthy) and `--update-max-failure-ratio`.

questions.q: A Swarm-deployed monitoring agent needs to run EXACTLY ONE replica on EVERY node in the Swarm — including any new nodes that join later. The agent's mode is 'global'. The complement is 'replicated' (a fixed number of replicas the scheduler distributes). Which describes global mode?
choices: A service that federates work across multiple separate Swarm clusters
A service that runs EXACTLY ONE task on EVERY node in the Swarm
A service that exposes external public IP access for every container in the Swarm
A service with an unlimited number of replicas distributed freely across every node
questions.explanation: Global mode services run exactly one task per node (similar to Kubernetes DaemonSets). As nodes join the Swarm, tasks are automatically scheduled on them. As nodes leave, tasks are cleaned up. Perfect for: node-level monitoring agents (Prometheus Node Exporter), log shippers (Fluentd), security scanners, or any workload that must run on every node. Create with: `docker service create --mode=global IMAGE`. used for monitoring agents, log shippers, and security scanners

questions.q: A Swarm has 5 managers. 3 of them go offline simultaneously (only 2 remain). The Raft consensus algorithm requires a MAJORITY (3 of 5) to commit state changes. With 2 managers, the Swarm CANNOT make state changes — existing services keep running, but no new tasks can be scheduled and no service updates accepted. Which describes manager / Raft + losing quorum?
choices: Losing any single manager immediately stops all scheduling and state changes
Worker nodes self-promote to managers when quorum is lost to restore Raft consensus
Managers only run workloads; workers handle Raft state consensus and scheduling
Managers use Raft consensus to maintain cluster state
questions.explanation: Swarm managers use Raft consensus to maintain a consistent distributed state store. For a cluster of N managers, quorum requires (N/2)+1 managers available. With quorum lost, the Swarm enters a read-only state — running containers continue, but no new services can be created, scaled, or updated. Recommendation: use 3 or 5 managers (tolerates 1 or 2 failures). Never use even numbers of managers. losing quorum (majority of managers) prevents scheduling changes — existing tasks continue but no new tasks can be scheduled

questions.q: A Swarm service `webapp` needs an `nginx.conf` that DIFFERS between dev / staging / prod. The config is NON-sensitive (no secrets). It should be mounted into the container as a file and managed centrally by Swarm — without rebuilding the image. Which Swarm feature?
choices: Bind mounts from NFS — possible but not Swarm-native
Env vars in Dockerfile — bakes config into image (anti-pattern for env-specific config)
Docker Configs
Per-env images — anti-pattern; rebuilds violate immutable-image principle
questions.explanation: Docker Configs (introduced in Docker 17.06) store non-sensitive configuration files in the Swarm's Raft log and mount them into containers at a specified path (similar to Secrets but for non-sensitive data). `docker config create nginx.conf nginx.conf` then `docker service create --config source=nginx.conf,target=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf nginx`. Configs are immutable; update by creating a new config version.

questions.q: In Docker Swarm, the default `ingress` overlay network enables the ROUTING MESH: any node in the Swarm can accept a published-port connection and route it (via the ingress overlay + IPVS) to a node running a task for that service. Clients can connect to ANY swarm IP and reach the service. Which describes ingress?
choices: Default overlay network that enables the routing mesh
Manager control-plane Raft network — the Raft consensus overlay carries internal manager-to-manager state sync but does not enable the routing mesh for published service ports
Monitoring network for Swarm health metrics
External load-balancer integration network
questions.explanation: The ingress network (created automatically with `docker swarm init`) enables the Swarm routing mesh. When a service publishes port 8080, EVERY Swarm node listens on port 8080. Traffic arriving on any node is load-balanced to a healthy task, regardless of which node the task runs on. This means you can point a load balancer at any node IP. Created as an overlay network with IPVS-based load balancing. allowing any Swarm node to receive traffic for a published service port and route it to a healthy task, regardless of which node runs the task

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: By default, when you `docker run nginx` without specifying a network, the container is attached to the `bridge` network. This is the standard SINGLE-HOST containerised network using a Linux bridge + iptables NAT for outbound and port-publish for inbound. Which network driver provides this single-host NAT-based behaviour?
choices: `none` driver — removes all networking; the container has no bridge interface and no connectivity, not even to the host
`bridge` driver
`overlay` driver — multi-host Swarm network using VXLAN encapsulation; not a single-host bridge-based driver
`host` driver — shares the host network namespace entirely; the container has no isolated bridge and sees all host interfaces directly
questions.explanation: The bridge driver (default for single-host) creates an isolated virtual network. Containers get private IPs and can communicate within the bridge network. Docker performs NAT so containers can reach the internet via the host. The host driver removes network isolation (container shares host's network stack). The overlay driver is for multi-host Swarm networking. none disables networking.

questions.q: Two containers on the SAME custom bridge network `mynet` can connect using `nslookup web` (each other by container name). The SAME two on the DEFAULT bridge network can NOT — name resolution fails. The reason is a fundamental difference between user-defined bridges and the default bridge. Which?
choices: The default `bridge` network does NOT have automatic DNS
Default bridge is IPv6-only
Requires Docker Compose
It does work on default bridge
questions.explanation: User-defined bridge networks include an embedded DNS server that resolves container names to their IPs. The default bridge network (docker0) does not have this — containers must use --link (deprecated) or IP addresses to communicate. This is a key reason to always create custom networks: automatic service discovery by name, better isolation, and network-level container grouping.

questions.q: A Docker SWARM has 3 manager + 5 worker nodes. A service deploys 10 replicas across the nodes. The replicas need to communicate as if on the same Layer-2 broadcast domain — but they're on DIFFERENT physical hosts. The Swarm-aware network driver builds an L2 OVERLAY by encapsulating frames in VXLAN. Which driver?
choices: `host` driver — direct host networking, no multi-host overlay
`overlay` driver
CDN-backed network
Single-node encrypted network
questions.explanation: Overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts (Swarm nodes), enabling containers on different physical/virtual machines to communicate using private IPs. Docker encapsulates traffic in VXLAN packets for host-to-host transport. Overlay networks are the foundation of Swarm service discovery and load balancing. They can be encrypted with --opt encrypted for node-to-node TLS.

questions.q: A security-tested container must run with NO NETWORK ACCESS WHATSOEVER — no DNS, no outbound, no inbound. The container should have a loopback interface only. Which Docker network driver?
choices: `bridge` network with `--icc=false` — disables inter-container communication on the bridge but the container still has a bridge interface and can reach external networks
`none` driver — gives the container ONLY a loopback interface; no external networking at all
`isolated`
`host` driver — exposes ALL host network interfaces to the container; the opposite of isolation, with no loopback-only restriction
questions.explanation: The 'none' network driver completely disables networking for the container. The container has only a loopback interface. Use it for containers processing local data with no network requirements (batch jobs, file processing), security-sensitive workloads, or containers that should not communicate with anything. `docker run --network=none myimage`.

questions.q: A running container `web` is currently only on the `frontend` network. The admin wants to ADD it to a `backend` network too — without restarting. Which Docker network command attaches a running container to an additional network?
choices: `docker container network-add`
`docker run --network=NETWORK` — set at RUN time, doesn't attach to a running one
`docker network connect <network> <container>`
`docker network join`
questions.explanation: `docker network connect NETWORK CONTAINER` attaches a running container to an additional network. The container immediately gets an IP address on that network. This is useful for connecting containers to multiple networks (e.g., a frontend network and a backend network). The reverse: `docker network disconnect NETWORK CONTAINER`.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: Docker Content Trust (DCT) protects against TAMPERING and IMPERSONATION of images. When DCT is enabled (`DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`), Docker only pulls / runs images whose tag is SIGNED by a trusted publisher. Notary is the signing backend. The signing key chain protects against man-in-the-middle or compromised registry attacks. Which describes DCT?
choices: Encrypts images at rest in Docker Hub
Requires two-factor authentication before images can be pulled
Uses digital signatures (via Notary) to verify images haven't been tampered with since publication
Scans images for CVE vulnerabilities — that is image vulnerability scanning (Snyk, Trivy, Hub scanning), separate from Notary-based content trust signing
questions.explanation: Docker Content Trust (DCT) uses The Update Framework (TUF) and Notary to sign and verify images. When enabled (DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1), Docker only pulls/runs images with valid signatures. It protects against: man-in-the-middle attacks substituting a legitimate image, running unverified third-party images, and supply chain tampering. Signers use offline root keys and online targets keys.

questions.q: A Swarm service `payments` needs the DB password. Hard-coding it in the image is unsafe. Env-vars are visible in `docker inspect`. The right approach: store the secret in the Swarm Raft log (encrypted at rest), make it available to the service as a FILE under `/run/secrets/db_password`, in-memory only on the worker. Which feature?
choices: Docker Secrets
Hardcode the password in the Docker image ENV instruction — an anti-pattern; the secret is baked into every image layer and visible via `docker history` and `docker inspect`
Pass the password as an environment variable in docker-compose — visible in `docker inspect` output on any node and not encrypted at rest in the Swarm Raft log
Mount a host directory containing the password file into the container — host-accessible and less secure than the Docker Secrets framework; not encrypted in the Swarm state
questions.explanation: Docker Secrets (Swarm only) stores sensitive data encrypted in the Swarm's Raft log. Secrets are decrypted and mounted as in-memory tmpfs files at /run/secrets/SECRET_NAME inside authorized containers — never written to disk. Environment variables are visible in `docker inspect` output and process listings. Hardcoding in images is an obvious anti-pattern. `docker secret create` and `docker service create --secret`.

questions.q: A web server container runs as root because it must bind to port 80 (privileged port < 1024). Best practice is to drop ALL Linux capabilities, then add back ONLY the specific capability needed to bind to low ports: `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`. The container becomes least-privileged. Which describes the effect?
choices: Prevents the container from ever becoming root and adds back full network admin capabilities via NET_ADMIN
Removes the AppArmor and seccomp security profiles from the container
Drops ALL Linux capabilities, then adds back ONLY `NET_BIND_SERVICE`
Disables all container networking and Linux kernel namespaces
questions.explanation: Linux capabilities break root privileges into distinct units. `--cap-drop ALL` removes all capabilities from the container. `--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` re-adds only the capability to bind to privileged ports (<1024). This follows the principle of least privilege — the container can run a web server on port 80 without any other elevated privileges. Never add SYS_ADMIN unless absolutely necessary. following the principle of least privilege

questions.q: A defence-in-depth pattern runs the container with its ROOT FILESYSTEM mounted READ-ONLY. The application writes to `tmpfs` mounts or volumes only. An attacker who gains code execution in the container CANNOT write to the rootfs (no malware drop, no log tampering). Which flag?
choices: `--read-only`
Image read-only
Prevents other containers reading
Configuration immutable
questions.explanation: `docker run --read-only myimage` mounts the container's root filesystem read-only. Any attempt to write to the container filesystem fails. This is a strong security control: (1) prevents malware from writing persistence mechanisms, (2) ensures all state is explicitly in volumes, (3) makes container behavior more predictable. Combine with `--tmpfs /tmp` for applications that need a temporary writable area. preventing any writes to the container layer — improves security and forces explicit volume usage for writable data

questions.q: Docker applies a default seccomp profile to every container. The profile RESTRICTS which Linux SYSTEM CALLS a container's processes can make (blocks dangerous ones like `kexec_load`, `reboot`, etc.). Custom profiles can be loaded with `--security-opt seccomp=profile.json`. Which describes seccomp?
choices: Encrypts inter-container traffic on the overlay network
Restricts which Linux SYSCALLS a container process can make
Restricts which Docker CLI commands each user is authorized to run — that is handled by Docker authorization plugins, not seccomp Linux syscall profiles
Limits container network bandwidth and QoS shaping — that requires tc/cgroups network rate limiting; seccomp is a Linux syscall filter unrelated to network bandwidth
questions.explanation: seccomp (secure computing mode) is a Linux kernel feature that filters syscalls. Docker applies a default seccomp profile blocking ~44 dangerous syscalls (e.g., keyctl, add_key, reboot). Custom profiles allow you to restrict further (whitelist-based) or allow more (for specific use cases). To disable: `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` (not recommended). Combined with namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, and AppArmor/SELinux for defense-in-depth.

nodes.title: Docker build and image layers: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Docker builds images layer by layer from a Dockerfile. Understanding the layer cache, multi-stage builds, and build context is essential for DCA exam questions on image size and build performance.

flashcards.front: What triggers a cache miss during docker build?
flashcards.back: Any change to a Dockerfile instruction or the files it COPYs invalidates that layer and all subsequent layers — order instructions from least to most frequently changed.

flashcards.front: Multi-stage build — main benefit?
flashcards.back: Compile or test in one stage using a full SDK image, then COPY only the binary/artifact into a minimal final stage — dramatically reduces final image size.

flashcards.front: docker build --no-cache — when to use?
flashcards.back: Forces a full rebuild from scratch, ignoring the layer cache. Useful when you need the latest base image or a fresh dependency fetch despite no Dockerfile changes.

flashcards.front: .dockerignore — purpose?
flashcards.back: Excludes files from the build context sent to the Docker daemon. Reduces build time and prevents accidentally baking secrets or large dev files into the image.

questions.q: A `Dockerfile` is in a repository alongside `node_modules/` (200 MB), `.git/` (50 MB), `*.log` files. Running `docker build .` sends ALL of those to the Docker daemon (the 'build context'). A file lets you EXCLUDE files from the build context (similar to `.gitignore`). Which?
choices: `.dockerignore`
Hidden env vars
Prevent Dockerfile instructions
Block image pulls
questions.explanation: The .dockerignore file works like .gitignore — it tells the Docker CLI which files and directories to exclude when sending the build context to the daemon. This speeds up builds (smaller context), prevents accidentally including secrets (e.g., .env, credentials), and avoids cache-busting from unrelated file changes.

questions.q: A Go service builds with `go build` into a 50 MB statically-linked binary. The build dependencies (go toolchain) are 800 MB. A SINGLE-stage Dockerfile produces an 800 MB image that includes the build toolchain. A MULTI-stage Dockerfile uses multiple FROM instructions: stage 1 builds the binary (uses the toolchain), stage 2 starts FROM scratch and COPYs ONLY the binary. The final image is ~50 MB. Which describes multi-stage builds?
choices: Multiple FROM instructions build multiple images simultaneously in parallel
Multiple FROM instructions in one Dockerfile separating build + runtime stages
Multiple FROM instructions define multiple OS platform targets for cross-compilation
Multiple FROM instructions implement conditional build logic using if/else branching
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM instructions. Build stages compile/test code with all required build tools. The final stage copies only the compiled artifacts, resulting in a minimal image without compilers, test frameworks, or intermediate files. For example, a Go app: stage 1 uses golang:alpine to compile, stage 2 uses scratch or alpine and copies just the binary — reducing image size from GB to MB. producing a smaller final image without build tools

questions.q: Docker builds REUSE cached layers when the instruction + its inputs are unchanged. A `COPY package.json /app/` followed by `RUN npm install` lets the npm install layer be CACHED as long as package.json doesn't change. Modifying package.json invalidates that layer AND every subsequent layer. Which describes Docker's layer cache behaviour?
choices: Whole image cached
Only RUN cached / COPY rebuilds
Each layer is cached individually
Tag-based cache
questions.explanation: Docker checks the cache by comparing each instruction and its context. If a COPY instruction's source files changed, that layer and all layers below it are rebuilt. Key optimization: put frequently changing instructions (COPY source code) AFTER infrequently changing ones (RUN apt-get install). This way, dependency installation is cached even when source code changes. `docker build --no-cache` bypasses all caching. a cache miss for any instruction (changed instruction or changed files it copies) invalidates the cache for that instruction AND all subsequent instructions

questions.q: Docker's newer build engine is BuildKit (set via `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1` or default in modern Docker). Improvements over the classic builder: (a) parallel build steps within a Dockerfile, (b) better caching (per-stage), (c) build secrets via `--secret`, (d) SSH agent forwarding via `--ssh`, (e) cross-platform builds via `--platform`, (f) `RUN --mount=type=cache` to share between builds. Which describes BuildKit?
choices: BuildKit replaces Docker Compose as the modern container orchestration tool
BuildKit is available on Windows hosts only for Windows container builds
BuildKit is a commercial-only add-on to Docker Enterprise requiring a paid license
Modern build subsystem
questions.explanation: BuildKit (enabled with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 or default in recent Docker versions) brings: concurrent layer building (faster multi-stage builds), intelligent cache management, `RUN --mount=type=secret` (secrets available at build time but NOT stored in the image), `RUN --mount=type=ssh` (SSH agent forwarding for private repos), better progress output, and inline cache. Use `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` at the top of your Dockerfile to enable all features. improved caching, secret mounts (never stored in layers), SSH forwarding, and smaller build contexts

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A MySQL container's data must SURVIVE: (a) container restart, (b) container removal, (c) Docker daemon restart, (d) host reboot. The data should live on the host's disk but be MANAGED by Docker (path, lifecycle, permissions). Which mount type?
choices: Container writable layer — managed by Docker but wiped on container removal; the opposite of durable persistence across restarts and host reboots
Named Docker volume — managed-by-Docker persistent storage; survives container removal; portable across containers; the canonical persistent storage
tmpfs mount — Docker-managed RAM-backed storage; data is lost when the container stops and is never written to host disk
Bind mount to /tmp on the host — works for persistence across container restarts but /tmp is volatile on most Linux systems (cleared at reboot) and is not Docker-managed
questions.explanation: Named Docker volumes are managed by Docker, portable, easy to back up, and work across different host paths. Bind mounts couple the container to a specific host path, reducing portability. tmpfs mounts are in-memory and lost when the container stops. The container's writable layer is removed with the container. Named volumes are the recommended production storage solution.

questions.q: Two persistent-storage mount types: (A) BIND MOUNT — host path mapped directly into container; managed by the host filesystem; great for dev (live-edit), less portable. (B) VOLUME — managed by Docker (`/var/lib/docker/volumes/`); portable; supports volume drivers (NFS, EBS, etc.); preferred for production. Which describes the difference?
choices: Docker volumes are read-only while bind mounts support read-write
Bind mounts only work on Linux hosts
Bind mount = specific host path mapped into the container (depends on
Bind mounts are faster than Docker volumes because a bind mount path bypasses the Docker storage layer — performance is comparable; portability is the key distinction
questions.explanation: Bind mounts: `docker run -v /host/path:/container/path` — tightly couples the container to a specific host directory. Great for development (live code editing) but reduces portability. Docker volumes: `docker run -v myvolume:/container/path` — Docker manages the storage location (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), independent lifecycle, easier to backup/migrate, work with volume drivers for cloud storage (EBS, NFS, etc.). Docker volumes are managed by Docker with their own lifecycle independent of containers

questions.q: A web container needs a SCRATCH directory for fast in-memory writes — temp files / sockets / session caches — that's WIPED when the container stops and never touches host disk. Use a RAM-backed mount. Which mount type fits?
choices: Compressed overlay filesystem mount for image layers
Read-only bind mount for sharing static assets between containers
`tmpfs` mount
On-disk BuildKit cache mount reused between build runs
questions.explanation: tmpfs mounts are stored in the host's memory only (never on disk). Data is temporary — lost when the container stops or restarts. Use cases: storing session tokens, credentials, or other sensitive data that should never touch disk; high-performance temporary scratch space. `docker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m myimage`. Available only on Linux. For secrets: use Docker Secrets in Swarm instead. data is never written to disk and is lost when the container stops; ideal for sensitive temporary data

questions.q: A container's CPU usage spikes to 100% on the host. The admin wants to LIMIT the container to 1.5 CPU shares + 512 MB memory. Docker enforces this via a LINUX KERNEL primitive that meters and limits resource usage per process group (CPU, memory, IO, pids). Which kernel feature?
choices: Linux namespaces — provide ISOLATION (pid, net, ipc, mount), not resource METERING
seccomp — restricts which syscalls a process can call, not resource limits
SELinux MAC — mandatory access control on files / processes; not resource limits
Control groups (cgroups)
questions.explanation: Control groups (cgroups) enforce resource limits: CPU shares, CPU quotas, memory limits, block I/O, network bandwidth. For example: `docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 myimage`. Linux namespaces provide isolation (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user namespaces). seccomp limits available syscalls. AppArmor/SELinux enforce MAC policies. Together, these form Docker's container isolation model.

questions.q: A container running on a Linux host sees its OWN process IDs (PID 1 is the container's entrypoint), its OWN network interfaces, its OWN filesystem root, its OWN user IDs. The Linux kernel feature providing each of these ISOLATED VIEWS is namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, USER, UTS, IPC, CGROUP). Which feature?
choices: cgroups (control groups) — the Linux kernel mechanism that meters and enforces resource limits (CPU, memory); not the feature that creates isolated namespaces for processes, networks, or filesystems
AppArmor — a Linux mandatory access control layer that applies per-process file and syscall policies; it does not create isolated namespaces for PID, network, or mount views
seccomp — a Linux kernel syscall filter that restricts permitted system calls; it does not create isolated namespaces for separate PID trees, network stacks, or filesystem roots
Linux namespaces
questions.explanation: Linux namespaces provide isolation at the kernel level. Docker uses: PID namespace (isolated process tree), Network namespace (isolated network stack, interfaces), Mount namespace (isolated filesystem), UTS namespace (isolated hostname), IPC namespace (isolated shared memory), User namespace (map container root to unprivileged host UID). Cgroups limit resources. seccomp limits syscalls. AppArmor/SELinux enforce access control policies.

questions.q: A developer asks 'are an image and a container the same thing?'. The SR engineer explains: ONE is a READ-ONLY artifact built from layered filesystem snapshots (stored in the registry / on disk). The OTHER is a RUNNING (or stopped) INSTANCE of that artifact with its own writable filesystem layer, namespaced PID + network, mounts, etc. Which mapping?
choices: Image = read-only layered filesystem template
Same thing
Images are for development, containers are for production
A container lives on disk while the image is held in memory
questions.explanation: A Docker image is an immutable, layered filesystem snapshot (read-only). A container is a live, running instance of that image with an additional thin writable layer (copy-on-write). Many containers can share the same underlying image layers, saving disk space. When a container is deleted, its writable layer is lost unless committed or using a volume. a container is a running instance of an image with a writable layer on top

questions.q: A team's images live on the public registry `hub.docker.com` (Docker Hub) AND on a self-hosted private registry `registry.company.com:5000`. The 'registry' is the SERVER-SIDE storage + distribution system. Docker Hub is just ONE OPERATOR's hosted instance of a registry. Which describes registries + Hub?
choices: A registry is the server-side image storage +
Docker Hub and a registry are synonyms
Docker Hub is open-source while a private registry is a commercial product
A registry server stores and serves container logs alongside images
questions.explanation: A Docker registry is any service that stores and serves Docker images using the Docker Registry HTTP API V2. Docker Hub is Docker's public hosted registry. Organizations run private registries for security/performance: Docker Trusted Registry (DTR, enterprise), Harbor, AWS ECR, GCR, Azure ACR. The registry is the infrastructure; Docker Hub is one implementation of it. Docker Hub is a specific public registry hosted by Docker Inc.

questions.q: A web container must be capped at 256 MB of memory and 0.5 vCPU (half a core). Which `docker run` flags?
choices: `--memory=256m --cpus=0.5` — canonical Docker resource limits; `--memory` (mem cap), `--cpus` (CPU quota as fraction of a core)
`--mem-limit --cpu-quota=50` — these are not real docker run flags; the correct flags are `--memory` for the memory cap and `--cpus` for fractional core allocation
`--ram --cpu=half` — these are not real docker run flags; Docker does not accept descriptive names like "half" for core fractions
`--memory=256 --cpu-shares=0.5` — `--memory=256` without a unit means 256 bytes, not 256 MB; `--cpu-shares` is a relative weight, not an absolute core fraction cap
questions.explanation: --memory=256m sets a hard memory limit (container OOM-killed if exceeded). --cpus=0.5 limits to half a CPU (equivalent to --cpu-quota=50000 --cpu-period=100000). Other useful flags: --memory-swap (total memory+swap limit), --cpu-shares (relative weight, soft limit), --oom-kill-disable (don't OOM kill, but risky). Always set memory limits in production to prevent one container starving others.
